 15535  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 15536  
 15537      \301\ See Irish Peace Process Cultural and Training Program Act 
 15538  of 1998, Public Law 105-319, 112 Stat. 3013 (Oct. 30, 1998), as 
 15539  amended by Public Law 108-449, 114 Stat. 1526 (Dec. 10, 2004).
 15540  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 15541  
 15542  D. EOS
 15543  
 15544      This final rule will not create a new form for an EOS application. 
 15545  However, in the future, some form names and numbers may change. While 
 15546  DHS plans to update existing forms to allow F and I nonimmigrants to 
 15547  apply for an EOS
 15548  
 15549  [[Page 45100]]
 15550  
 15551  with USCIS, DHS believes it is more efficient to replace references to 
 15552  specific form names and numbers throughout the current regulations with 
 15553  generally applicable language.
 15554      Using general language in the regulatory text instead of referring 
 15555  to specific form names and numbers helps both DHS and stakeholders. It 
 15556  allows for technical changes without requiring an entirely new 
 15557  rulemaking to update form names. Stakeholders will receive notice and 
 15558  specific guidance on USCIS' website and in the appropriate form 
 15559  instructions, as they already do for various other benefits. Therefore, 
 15560  DHS uses this language in 8 CFR 214.1(c)(2) and struck the phrase 
 15561  exempting F and J nonimmigrants from filing an EOS, as they will be 
 15562  required to file an EOS if they wish to remain in the United States 
 15563  beyond their specified date of admission. See new 8 CFR 214.1(c)(2).
 15564      Additionally, DHS struck ``other than as provided in 214.2(f)(7)'' 
 15565  from new 8 CFR 214.1(c)(3)(v) and added in its place ``except those who 
 15566  fall under 8 CFR 214.1(m)'' to make it clear that students must apply 
 15567  for an EOS. This requirement will not apply to other nonimmigrants 
 15568  admitted for D/S, such as A-1 or A-2 representatives of foreign 
 15569  governments and their immediate family members; they will remain 
 15570  ineligible to file an EOS.
 15571      As part of the EOS application, USCIS requires biometric collection 
 15572  and may require such collection from F, J, and I nonimmigrants. USCIS 
 15573  has the general authority to require and collect biometrics from 
 15574  applicants, petitioners, sponsors, beneficiaries, or other individuals 
 15575  residing in the United States for any immigration and naturalization 
 15576  benefit. See 8 CFR 103.16. Biometric collection helps USCIS confirm an 
 15577  individual's identity and conduct background and security checks. 
 15578  Further, USCIS may also require any applicant, petitioner, sponsor, 
 15579  beneficiary or individual filing a benefit request, or any group or 
 15580  class of such persons submitting requests to appear for an interview. 
 15581  See 8 CFR 103.2(b)(9). USCIS may require such an interview as part of 
 15582  the screening and adjudication process that helps confirm an 
 15583  individual's identity, elicit information to assess the eligibility for 
 15584  an immigration benefit, and screen for any national security or fraud 
 15585  concerns.
 15586      The rule addresses the admission of F, J, and I nonimmigrants who 
 15587  timely filed an EOS and/or an application for employment authorization 
 15588  but left the United States before receiving a decision from USCIS. DHS 
 15589  anticipates this scenario will apply mostly to F-1 students applying 
 15590  for post-completion OPT and STEM OPT extensions.
 15591      While USCIS generally does not consider an application for EOS 
 15592  abandoned when the nonimmigrant leaves the United States,\302\ DHS 
 15593  recognizes the potential for conflict if a nonimmigrant receives 
 15594  authorization from both CBP and USCIS for what amounts to the same 
 15595  request (a specific period of time to pursue authorized activities). 
 15596  Where an alien in F, J, or I status timely files an application for 
 15597  EOS, leaves the United States before USCIS approves that EOS 
 15598  application, and applies for admission to continue his or her 
 15599  activities for the balance of the previously authorized admission 
 15600  period, USCIS would generally not consider the EOS application 
 15601  abandoned. See new 8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(i).
 15602  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 15603  
 15604      \302\ See U.S. Dep't of Justice, Memo from Cook, Acting Asst. 
 15605  Comm. Programs, Travel After Filing a Request for a Change of 
 15606  Nonimmigrant Status, HQ 70/6.2.9 (June 18, 2001), https://www.uscis.gov/sites/default/files/document/memos/Travpub.pdf.
 15607  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 15608  
 15609      Consistent with the general provision on admission in new 8 CFR 
 15610  214.1(a)(4) where the alien leaves the United States and applies for 
 15611  admission while his or her EOS application is pending and is admitted 
 15612  based on a new Form I-20 or DS-2019 after his or her previously 
 15613  authorized admission has expired; the pending EOS may be deemed 
 15614  abandoned. In this case, the AUD provided by CBP on the alien's I-94 
 15615  would govern. See new 8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(ii). This is because, in these 
 15616  cases, CBP's grant of a new period of authorized stay will supersede 
 15617  the pending EOS application seeking a period of authorized stay, 
 15618  rendering it superfluous.
 15619      DHS considered a policy whereby an F, J, or I nonimmigrant would 
 15620  automatically abandon an EOS application upon departing the United 
 15621  States. However, DHS believes such a strict requirement would not be 
 15622  practical, because people cannot always predict when they will have to 
 15623  travel. The decision to grant or deny an EOS, including in the event of 
 15624  a departure, involves an exercise of agency discretion, utilizing the 
 15625  laws, regulations, agency policy, and operational guidance.
 15626      Regarding applications for employment authorization for F-1 and J-2 
 15627  nonimmigrants, DHS notes that CBP does not adjudicate applications for 
 15628  employment authorization. Should an EOS application be deemed 
 15629  abandoned, USCIS will continue processing any applications for 
 15630  employment authorization, notwithstanding a departure, and, if the 
 15631  application is approved, USCIS will not issue an EAD with a validity 
 15632  date that exceeds the fixed date of admission provided to the alien at 
 15633  the POE. For example, an F-1 student wishing to engage in post-
 15634  completion OPT or a STEM OPT extension will need to file both an EOS 
 15635  application and an application for employment authorization. Where the 
 15636  alien had departed the United States before his or her applications are 
 15637  adjudicated, USCIS will not consider the employment authorization 
 15638  application abandoned. See new 8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(ii).
 15639      In all events, when an F-1 or a J-2 nonimmigrant travels while the 
 15640  employment authorization or EOS application is pending, he or she is 
 15641  still expected to respond to any RFE and to timely submit the requested 
 15642  documents. Because an RFE may arrive after an alien departs, either 
 15643  electronically or at a U.S. address, aliens traveling outside the 
 15644  United States while applications are pending are advised to make 
 15645  necessary arrangements to determine whether they have received an RFE 
 15646  relating to their application and to timely respond to any RFE.\303\ 
 15647  Failure to do so could result in USCIS denying an employment 
 15648  authorization or EOS application for abandonment.
 15649  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 15650  
 15651      \303\ See ICE, Traveling as an International Student, https://studyinthestates.dhs.gov/traveling-as-an-international-student (last 
 15652  visited Feb. 9, 2026). See also ICE, Travelling Outside the United 
 15653  States for Five Months or Fewer, https://www.ice.gov/sevis/travel 
 15654  (last updated July 8, 2025), which notes, ``Can I reenter if my 
 15655  request for OPT is pending? Yes, but traveling during this time 
 15656  should be undertaken with caution. USCIS may send you [an RFE] while 
 15657  you are away, however, so you will want to make sure you have 
 15658  provided a correct U.S. address both to your DSO and on the 
 15659  application and would be able to send in requested documents. Also, 
 15660  if USCIS approves your OPT application, you will be expected to have 
 15661  your EAD in hand to re-enter the United States. Like a request for 
 15662  further information, USCIS can only send the EAD to your U.S. 
 15663  address.''
 15664  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 15665  
 15666  E. Transition Period
 15667  
 15668  1. F and J Nonimmigrants Who Are in D/S on the Effective Date of the 
 15669  Final Rule
 15670      DHS will generally allow all F and J nonimmigrants present in the 
 15671  United States on the final rule's effective date who are validly 
 15672  maintaining that status and who were admitted for D/S to remain in the 
 15673  United States in F or J status, without filing an EOS request, up to 
 15674  the program end date reflected on their Form I-20 or DS-2019 that is 
 15675  valid on the final rule's effective date, for a period not to exceed 4 
 15676  years from the effective date of the final rule, plus an additional 60 
 15677  days for these F nonimmigrants and 30 days for J
 15678  
 15679  [[Page 45101]]
 15680  
 15681  nonimmigrants to depart the country. See new 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1).
 15682      F and J nonimmigrants who depart the United States after the rule's 
 15683  effective date and before the end date reflected on their Form I-20 or 
 15684  DS-2019 may be admitted with a new fixed admission period, like any 
 15685  other newly admitted F or J nonimmigrant, as provided for in new 8 CFR 
 15686  214.1(a)(4), based on the date on their Form I-20 or DS-2019 and 30 
 15687  days for departure. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5) or (j)(1)(ii). Aliens who 
 15688  need additional time to complete their current course of study, 
 15689  including requests for post-completion OPT, STEM OPT, or academic 
 15690  training, or would like to start a new course of study or exchange 
 15691  visitor program must apply for an EOS with USCIS for an admission 
 15692  period up to the new program end date, or OPT end date, listed on the 
 15693  Form I-20 or DS-2019, or successor form, reflecting such an extension, 
 15694  up to a maximum of 4-years. See new 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1).
 15695      For those aliens in F-1 status, admitted for D/S, present in the 
 15696  United States on September 15, 2026 who have timely filed on or before 
 15697  September 15, 2026 an application for post-completion OPT or a STEM OPT 
 15698  extension, there is not a requirement to file an EOS application, and, 
 15699  instead, they are only required to file the application for employment 
 15700  authorization for post-completion OPT or STEM OPT extension. See new 8 
 15701  CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i). An F-1 nonimmigrant who departs the United States 
 15702  before filing the application for post-completion OPT or STEM OPT, and 
 15703  is subsequently admitted to the United States with a fixed period of 
 15704  admission is required to file both an application for employment 
 15705  authorization, (Form I-765 or successor form) and an Application to 
 15706  Extend/Change Nonimmigrant Status (Form I-539, or successor form), 
 15707  pursuant to 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(i)(B)(2) or (C). See new 8 CFR 
 15708  214.1(m)(1)(ii). An alien described in this section who departs the 
 15709  United States while the Application for Employment Authorization is 
 15710  pending or once approved will be admitted for a fixed period of time 
 15711  pursuant to 8 CFR 214.1(a). Id. DHS reserves the discretion to extend 
 15712  the period exempting the filing of the Application to Extend/Change 
 15713  Nonimmigrant Status (Form I-539 or successor form) in 6-month 
 15714  increments by publication of a notice in the Federal Register. See new 
 15715  8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(iii). The final rule moved this paragraph from 
 15716  paragraph (ii) to offer additional clarity, since such an extension can 
 15717  also apply to paragraph (i).
 15718      An F-1 nonimmigrant who departs the United States while the 
 15719  application for employment authorization for post-completion OPT or 
 15720  STEM OPT is pending or once approved will be admitted for a fixed 
 15721  admission period pursuant to new 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(iii). F-1 
 15722  nonimmigrants who file for employment authorization for STEM OPT remain 
 15723  eligible for the 180-day extension of their post-completion OPT EAD 
 15724  while their application for STEM OPT is pending pursuant to 8 CFR 
 15725  274a.12(b)(6)(iv).
 15726      Regarding pending applications for employment authorization during 
 15727  the transition period, aliens in F status who are subject to the 
 15728  transition and who are seeking post-completion OPT and STEM OPT 
 15729  employment authorization will be authorized to lawfully remain in the 
 15730  United States while the application is pending with USCIS if: (1) they 
 15731  are in the United States on the effective date of the final rule with 
 15732  admission for D/S; (2) they properly filed an application for 
 15733  employment authorization; (3) their application is pending on the final 
 15734  rule's effective date; and (4) they are not otherwise removable under 
 15735  the INA. Unless otherwise advised by USCIS, they will not have to file 
 15736  for an EOS or re-file an application for employment authorization. See 
 15737  new 8 CFR 214.1(m)(2). If the application for employment authorization 
 15738  is approved, the F-1 student will be authorized to remain in the United 
 15739  States in F-1 status until the expiration date of the EAD, plus 60 days 
 15740  as provided in their previous admission. If the employment application 
 15741  is denied, the F-1 student will continue to be authorized to remain in 
 15742  the United States until the program end date listed on their Form I-20, 
 15743  plus 60 days as provided in their previous admission, as long as he or 
 15744  she continues to pursue a full course of study and otherwise meets the 
 15745  requirements for F-1 status. See new 8 CFR 214.1(m)(2)(i).
 15746      Aliens in F-1 status with pending employment authorization 
 15747  applications, other than post-completion OPT and STEM OPT, also do not 
 15748  need to file for an extension or refile an employment authorization 
 15749  application. As long as these F-1 nonimmigrants continue to meet the 
 15750  requirements for F-1 status, they continue to be authorized to remain 
 15751  in the United States until the program end date listed on the Form I-
 15752  20, plus 60 days, regardless of whether the employment authorization is 
 15753  approved or denied. See new 8 CFR 214.1(m)(2)(ii).
 15754      As discussed in the NPRM, DHS believes that this transition will 
 15755  not be unreasonably burdensome on F and J nonimmigrants, and it will 
 15756  enable DHS to transition F and J nonimmigrants without unduly burdening 
 15757  nonimmigrants, USCIS, or CBP. Many would be able to complete their 
 15758  programs per the terms of their initial D/S using the original program 
 15759  end date as an expiration of their authorized period of stay. DHS may 
 15760  grant such periods, which include an additional 60 days for F 
 15761  nonimmigrants and 30 days for J nonimmigrants as provided in their 
 15762  previous admission, automatically without an application or fee. With 
 15763  this option, DHS believes that the majority of F and J nonimmigrants 
 15764  will be shifted to a fixed initial period of admission of 4 years or 
 15765  less. For example, J-1 research scholars and alien physicians who have 
 15766  program end dates for up to 5 or 7 years respectively will need to 
 15767  apply for an EOS before the 4-year maximum period of stay expires, 
 15768  i.e., the date that falls 4 years after the rule becomes effective and 
 15769  is listed in this rule for each program.
 15770      This will also allow DHS to transition F and J nonimmigrants to an 
 15771  admission for a fixed time period without unduly burdening them, USCIS, 
 15772  or CBP. It ensures that no F and J nonimmigrants remain in the United 
 15773  States indefinitely by requiring all F and J nonimmigrants admitted for 
 15774  D/S who wish to extend their stay beyond their program end date or the 
 15775  4-year maximum, whichever is applicable, to either file an EOS request 
 15776  or depart the United States and apply for admission at a POE by their 
 15777  program end date or the 4-year maximum period of stay from the 
 15778  effective date of this final rule, plus an additional 60 days for F 
 15779  nonimmigrants and 30 days for J nonimmigrants.
 15780      DHS considered the effect of transitioning to a fixed period of 
 15781  admission on F and J nonimmigrants originally admitted for D/S who 
 15782  chose to temporarily come to the United States to pursue a program of 
 15783  study or an exchange visitor program. DHS believes the changes will not 
 15784  significantly affect the interests of these nonimmigrants admitted in 
 15785  D/S. DHS is not changing the fundamental requirements to qualify for 
 15786  these nonimmigrant statuses, rather it is only changing the length of 
 15787  time that an individual may lawfully remain in the United States in F 
 15788  or J status without filing an EOS application. Admitting these 
 15789  classifications of nonimmigrants for a fixed period of admission simply 
 15790  confirms that the admission is temporary and clearly communicates when 
 15791  that temporary admission period ends. Further, as is the case for the 
 15792  fixed period of admission policy more generally, a fixed date of 
 15793  admission simply places these
 15794  
 15795  [[Page 45102]]
 15796  
 15797  nonimmigrants in the same position as most other nonimmigrants who are 
 15798  temporarily in the United States. They will still be able to continue 
 15799  to pursue their full course of study or exchange program; however, if 
 15800  they need additional time in F or J status, the burden will now be on 
 15801  them to request authorization directly from DHS and establish 
 15802  eligibility to extend their period of stay in such status, whereas 
 15803  previously they obtained an extension of lawful status in conjunction 
 15804  with a program extension through a DSO or RO.
 15805      At the same time, this process will provide immigration officials 
 15806  an opportunity to directly review and determine whether F and J 
 15807  nonimmigrants who wish to remain in the United States beyond their 
 15808  fixed period of admission are complying with U.S. immigration law and 
 15809  are indeed eligible to retain their nonimmigrant status. If there are F 
 15810  or J nonimmigrants relying on a D/S admission in an attempt to 
 15811  permanently remain in the United States, or otherwise circumvent their 
 15812  authorized status, this process will allow DHS to detect and deny an 
 15813  EOS request or entry under a new period of admission. DHS considered 
 15814  several alternatives in the NPRM before determining the above proposal 
 15815  was the best option.\304\
 15816  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 15817  
 15818      \304\ 90 FR at 42085-86 (Aug. 28, 2025).
 15819  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 15820

 15822  Rule
 15823      I nonimmigrants who are in the United States on the effective date 
 15824  of the final rule will change from the existing D/S admission to a 
 15825  fixed date of admission. DHS is adopting the proposal in the NPRM for 
 15826  an automatic extension of the length of time it takes the alien to 
 15827  complete his or her activity, for a period of up to 240 days. See new 8 
 15828  CFR 214.1(m)(3). This is based on the period of stay authorized in 8 
 15829  CFR 274a.12(b)(20), which generally provides an automatic extension of 
 15830  employment authorization of 240 days to certain aliens whose status has 
 15831  expired but on whose behalf an application for an EOS was timely filed 
 15832  through a Form I-539, Application to Extend/Change Nonimmigrant Status, 
 15833  and which under new 8 CFR 214.2(i), has been generally applicable to an 
 15834  I nonimmigrant who changes information mediums.\305\ However, aliens 
 15835  who present a passport issued by the People's Republic of China (with 
 15836  the exception of a Hong Kong SAR passport or a Macau SAR passport), may 
 15837  be authorized an EOS until the activities or assignments consistent 
 15838  with the I classification are completed, but the EOS must not exceed 
 15839  the maximum period of 90 days. See new 8 CFR 214.1(m)(3). DHS believes 
 15840  that adopting an already established timeframe, to which I 
 15841  nonimmigrants are already accustomed, is reasonable. Consistent with 
 15842  the current process, an I nonimmigrant who departs the United States 
 15843  after the effective date of this final rule and would like to return to 
 15844  the United States in that same status will need to reapply for 
 15845  admission as an I nonimmigrant at a POE.

 15847  
 15848      \305\ See USCIS, Instructions for Application to Extend/Change 
 15849  Nonimmigrant Status, https://www.uscis.gov/i-539 (last updated Jan. 
 15850  9, 2026).
 15851  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 15852  
 15853      I nonimmigrants on D/S who seek to remain in the United States 
 15854  longer than the automatic extension period provided are required to 
 15855  file an EOS request with USCIS. \306\ Id. In addition to I 
 15856  nonimmigrants being familiar with the timeframe under 8 CFR 
 15857  274a.12(b)(20), DHS anticipates that this provision will reduce any 
 15858  gaps in employment due to USCIS' processing timeframes between the I 
 15859  nonimmigrant's application for extension and USCIS approval of the 
 15860  application. It will also facilitate an I nonimmigrant's ability to 
 15861  complete his or her assignment while temporarily in the United States 
 15862  on behalf of a foreign media organization, it that it will give ample 
 15863  time to any I nonimmigrant to either complete that assignment or ask 
 15864  for an extension, as needed.
 15865  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 15866  
 15867      \306\ In FY 2024, fewer than 38,000 aliens entered the U.S. in I 
 15868  classification. See DHS FY 2024, Quarter 4, tbl.4B, supra note 11.
 15869  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 15870  
 15871      If the EOS is denied, the alien must cease working and depart the 
 15872  United States immediately. As with most other nonimmigrant 
 15873  classifications, they will not be given any period of time to prepare 
 15874  for departure from the United States after the denial, and there may be 
 15875  significant immigration consequences for failing to depart the country 
 15876  immediately. For example, such aliens generally will begin to accrue 
 15877  unlawful presence the day after the issuance of the denial. DHS 
 15878  believes this standard provides parity across nonimmigrant 
 15879  classifications.
 15880      Finally, the transition procedures do not apply to aliens in F, J, 
 15881  or I nonimmigrant status who are outside the United States when the 
 15882  final rule takes effect, or to any aliens present in the United States 
 15883  in violation of their status. See 8 CFR 214.1(m).

tools.name: fr_search

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".
query.title: Query

doc_type.description: Document types: RULE, PRORULE (proposed rule), NOTICE, PRESDOCU (presidential document). null for all.

agency.description: Agency slugs, e.g. homeland-security-department, u-s-citizenship-and-immigration-services, u-s-immigration-and-customs-enforcement, state-department, labor-department, executive-office-of-the-president.
agency.title: Agency

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).
pres_type.title: Pres Type

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.
cfr.title: Cfr

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...
answer.title: Answer

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.
basis.title: Basis

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".

agency.description: Agency slugs, e.g. homeland-security-department, u-s-citizenship-and-immigration-services, u-s-immigration-and-customs-enforcement, state-department, labor-department, executive-office-of-the-president.
agency.title: Agency

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).
pres_type.title: Pres Type

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.
cfr.title: Cfr

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...
answer.title: Answer

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.

 13500      Comments: One commenter remarked that, given the financial burden 
 13501  and uncertainty associated with international travel, exiting and 
 13502  reentering the United States at a POE would not be a viable alternative 
 13503  to filing Form I-539 with USCIS for extending status. The commenter 
 13504  also stated that F-1 and J-1 visa holders, particularly individuals 
 13505  holding single-entry visas, may need to obtain a new visa stamp to 
 13506  travel abroad and reenter the country to extend their period of 
 13507  admission. This may force individuals to remain outside the United 
 13508  States for an extended period of time and impose significant personal 
 13509  cost and risk.
 13510      Response: DHS acknowledges that travelling outside of the United 
 13511  States and re-entering may not be the preferred option for all impacted 
 13512  visa holders. The exact proportion of eligible nonimmigrants who will 
 13513  choose to re-enter through a POE is unknown, but in the regulatory 
 13514  impact analysis for the NPRM and Final Rule, DHS assumes that, while 
 13515  requesting an EOS at a POE is an option, many nonimmigrants wishing to 
 13516  remain in the country will file an EOS and remain in country instead of 
 13517  incurring costs due to travel and reentry. The regulatory impact 
 13518  analysis also assesses how the impacts would change if nonimmigrants 
 13519  sought extensions while traveling through a POE instead of filing the 
 13520  I-539 or I-539A form.
 13521  (3) Unquantifiable and Intangible Costs
 13522      Comments: One commenter stated that DHS does not acknowledge the 
 13523  unquantifiable and intangible costs associated with the uncertainty of 
 13524  applying for a new period of admission. These include (1) the lack of 
 13525  published adjudication data for Form I-539 to inform the likelihood of 
 13526  EOS denial under the proposed rule, (2) current processing time issues 
 13527  at the USCIS California Service Center, which reports an average of 4.5 
 13528  months for changes to F-1 or J-1 status and 3.5 months for extensions, 
 13529  and (3) the inability of applicants to depart the United States after 
 13530  filing an EOS application for fear of abandoning the application and 
 13531  losing their money.
 13532      Response: DHS acknowledges that a denial of EOS may cause an 
 13533  interruption in a student's studies. However, any such denial would be 
 13534  warranted due to an applicant's lack of eligibility for an EOS (i.e., 
 13535  the student is placed on academic probation or suspension, repeatedly 
 13536  fails classes, failed to maintain their nonimmigrant status, or has a 
 13537  criminal history).
 13538      DHS acknowledges backlogs in the processing of EOS applications 
 13539  have occurred due to various factors not related to this rulemaking. 
 13540  DHS believes that factors contributing to this backlog will not be 
 13541  present when more significant influx of EOS applications resulting from 
 13542  this final rule are anticipated to be filed with USCIS. USCIS, as a fee 
 13543  funded agency, may set fees to support the additional workload 
 13544  associated with adjudication of cases subject to section 212(a)(4) of 
 13545  the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(4). USCIS conducts comprehensive fee studies 
 13546  on a biennial basis to assess whether its fee schedule adequately 
 13547  accounts for the full cost of naturalization and adjudication services. 
 13548  This assessment necessarily takes into account the projected volume of 
 13549  filings and the level of effort necessary to adjudicate various 
 13550  immigration benefit requests.\276\ USCIS will allocate appropriate 
 13551  levels of resources to ensure the adjudication of EOS continues in a 
 13552  timely fashion. Due to the expected growth of fees paid for the I-539 
 13553  form, USCIS will have more resources to allocate to meet the demand.
 13554  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 13555  
 13556      \276\ USCIS published a rule to change its fee schedule. See 
 13557  USCIS Fee Schedule and Changes to Certain Other Immigration Benefit 
 13558  Request Requirements, 85 FR 46788 (Aug. 3, 2020), corrected by USCIS 
 13559  Fee Schedule and Changes to Certain Other Immigration Benefit 
 13560  Request Requirements, 85 FR 49941 (Aug. 17, 2020) (Fee Rule). The

 13595  USCIS.
 13596      Comments: Multiple commenters stated that DHS failed to quantify 
 13597  the economic and operational impact of the proposed rule on USCIS, 
 13598  despite the agency potentially needing to process hundreds of thousands 
 13599  of additional EOS applications. Without evidence, these comments stated 
 13600  that USCIS currently lacks the necessary systems, staffing, training, 
 13601  information technology (IT) infrastructure, and integration 
 13602  capabilities to manage such an increase in application volume 
 13603  efficiently. One commenter highlighted that USCIS is already facing 
 13604  significant resource constraints and processing delays, particularly 
 13605  after the recent loss of experienced personnel due to government 
 13606  downsizing and added that further workload increases without adequate 
 13607  resources would likely strain the agency and lead to longer processing 
 13608  times. Another commenter recommended that DHS fully assess the 
 13609  potential impact of the proposed rule on application processing times 
 13610  across all Federal agencies, particularly those responsible for 
 13611  employment-based applications.

 13613  in fee-paying volumes of EOS applications received by USCIS following 
 13614  the effective date of the final rule as those nonimmigrants who are

 13616  However, DHS notes that the most significant increase in the volume of 
 13617  EOS applications will not materialize until 4 years after the effective 
 13618  date of this rule. This will allow time for DHS to shift resources as 
 13619  needed and as appropriate to ensure that the larger increased volumes 
 13620  are integrated into existing workflows. Several commenters noted and 
 13621  DHS has acknowledged backlogs in the processing of EOS applications. 
 13622  DHS believes that, given that 80 percent of Form I-539 adjudications 
 13623  for F, M, and J aliens are completed in three months,\277\ factors 
 13624  contributing to this backlog will not be present when the EOS 
 13625  applications resulting from this final rule are anticipated to be filed 
 13626  with USCIS. The fees collected with the increase in applications will 
 13627  result in additional resources for USCIS to use to mitigate the impact 
 13628  on the processing queue. The funds can be used to allocate appropriate 
 13629  resources to ensure adjudication of the I-539 in a timely manner. This 
 13630  will lessen the impact on processing times for applications with USCIS.

  8450      Response: Undergraduate students seeking to transfer to another 
  8451  school or change their educational objectives during their first year 
  8452  of study still retain flexibility in having their cases reviewed by 
  8453  DHS, which may then authorize the change in educational objective or 
  8454  school transfer if an exception is warranted. Transfers to other 
  8455  schools or changing majors after the first year of study is allowed at 
  8456  the undergraduate level, including for students who do not meet certain 
  8457  requirements to progress within their program and change majors. Any 
  8458  graduate student that fails out of the program will need to return 
  8459  home.
  8460      This particular change seeks to address significant costs incurred 
  8461  by universities when working with potential F-1 students who then 
  8462  transfer to less expensive schools upon arrival in the United States. 
  8463  This provision will provide more stability in the admission process and 
  8464  still provides the students with the ability to explore coursework and 
  8465  majors during the first year. Most undergraduate students take similar 
  8466  classes in their first year; therefore, the majority of the commenters' 
  8467  objections about changing degrees in the first year are not a concern 
  8468  under this new framework.
  8469  f. Program Changes for Graduate Students
  8470      Comments: Commenters stated that changes to graduate programs do 
  8471  not account for actual experiences of students. The majority of 
  8472  commenters expressed opposition to the proposed rule's prohibition on 
  8473  F-1 graduate students changing programs or educational objectives 
  8474  during their program of study. Commenters expressed particular concern 
  8475  about the impact on Ph.D. students, remarking that the proposed 
  8476  restrictions demonstrate a lack of understanding about the nature of 
  8477  graduate education, which often involves interdisciplinary work and 
  8478  evolving research interests.
  8479      Commenters stated that the rule would disrupt common practices in 
  8480  graduate education, including master's students being promoted to Ph.D. 
  8481  programs midway through their studies, Ph.D. students receiving 
  8482  master's degrees enroute to their doctorate, and students pursuing dual 
  8483  degrees at the graduate level. Another commenter expressed the proposed 
  8484  rule would eliminate the ``master-out'' option for Ph.D. students who 
  8485  are awarded a master's degree when they cannot finish, and harm 
  8486  ``academic mobility'' for second master's degrees and master's-out 
  8487  pathways. Commenters clarified that graduate school, particularly at 
  8488  the doctoral level, is not a fixed, linear path, and intellectual 
  8489  discovery often leads students to pivot to related fields. Commenters 
  8490  stated that the rule would punish academic growth by causing students 
  8491  to abandon years of work rather than transition programs. Many 
  8492  commenters expressed concern with the proposed rule's different 
  8493  provisions for graduate students compared to undergraduate students, 
  8494  noting that the proposed rule lacks explanation or rationale for these 
  8495  distinctions. One commenter reported extenuating and uncontrollable 
  8496  circumstances may cause a graduate student to transfer programs or 
  8497  institutions, while another commenter thought the proposed rule would 
  8498  punish students for issues beyond their control by locking students 
  8499  into a major their first year and by requiring graduate students to 
  8500  remain in their program. Another commenter stated that the proposed 
  8501  rule would make Ph.D. enrollment riskier and would leave open teaching 
  8502  assistant and research positions that are dependent on foreign 
  8503  students.
  8504      Commenters provided numerous reasons why graduate students might 
  8505  need to change programs, including refined research direction, changes 
  8506  in advisors, moves from master's to doctoral programs, suggestions from 
  8507  faculty members, personal or academic circumstances, and changes in 
  8508  research funding. Commenters emphasized the critical relationship 
  8509  between graduate students and their faculty advisors, explaining that 
  8510  students often choose specific institutions because of faculty members 
  8511  whose research aligns with their interests, reasoning that when faculty 
  8512  members relocate to another university, graduate students may need to 
  8513  transfer to continue working with their chosen mentors and maintain 
  8514  access to specialized research facilities. Commenters noted that 
  8515  research funding is often tied to specific faculty members, requiring 
  8516  students to follow their advisors to maintain financial support.
  8517      Commenters urged DHS to reconsider its restrictions on graduate 
  8518  students seeking to transfer or change educational objectives, with 
  8519  specific requests to allow Ph.D. students the option to transfer, 
  8520  particularly in cases involving academic or financial necessity. If DHS 
  8521  proceeds with finalizing the rule, commenters suggested establishing 
  8522  exceptions, such as allowing students to transfer to continue 
  8523  mentorship with their advisor, and proposed simplifying procedures for 
  8524  program extensions and transfers, especially at the graduate level. 
  8525  Commenters asked what happens after the 240-day authorized stay ends 
  8526  while an application is pending, the earliest filing date for 
  8527  applications, and how Ph.D. students whose programs exceed four years 
  8528  would justify extensions.
  8529      Commenters noted the rule could prevent individuals who completed a 
  8530  Ph.D. from later enrolling in a U.S. MD program or vice versa, despite 
  8531  these degrees preparing students for distinct career paths. Commenters 
  8532  expressed concern about uncertainty for medical residents on F-1 visas 
  8533  regarding whether residency would be considered a higher education 
  8534  level than medical school, potential barriers to changing disciplines 
  8535  during residency, and disruptions to transitions between PharmD 
  8536  programs or movement from PharmD to research-focused graduate programs.
  8537      Relatedly, a few commenters noted that the changes would prohibit 
  8538  students from pursuing a second master's degree which could hamper 
  8539  their ability to shift careers and add interdisciplinary training. One 
  8540  commenter pursuing a second STEM master's degree also expressed concern 
  8541  for the uncertainty surrounding using OPT after a second master's 
  8542  degree and stated that this might direct students away from the United 
  8543  States. Another commenter spoke about how the inability to pursue a 
  8544  second master's degree may hamper a student from ``applied, industry-
  8545  ready training.''
  8546      Response: DHS acknowledges that students may seek to engage in 
  8547  programs simultaneously at a lower level or obtain multiple degrees, at 
  8548  differing levels, throughout the course of their time in the United 
  8549  States. Students will be able to continue earning such credentials 
  8550  while also making progress in the degree program for which they have 
  8551  been issued a Form I-20. For example, a student issued a Form I-20 for 
  8552  a Ph.D. program as their primary academic objective could obtain a 
  8553  master's degree incidental to
  8554  
  8555  [[Page 45043]]
  8556  
  8557  status while progressing toward completion of the Ph.D. program.
  8558      DHS generally relies on NCES' definition of educational levels, 
  8559  which provides a structure for determining whether a nonimmigrant 
  8560  student's program of study reflects upward academic progression. The 
  8561  list of educational levels that schools use to update their Form I-17, 
  8562  ``Petition for Approval of School for Attendance by Nonimmigrant 
  8563  student,'' is available at https://studyinthestates.dhs.gov/sevis-help-hub/school-records/school-certification/form-i-17-listing-of-available-degrees. This list contains the following educational levels: 1. 
  8564  Primary and Secondary Education; 2. ELT; 3. Post-secondary 
  8565  Certificates/Non-Degree; 4. Associate; 5. Bachelor; 6. Master; 7. 
  8566  Doctorate. DHS may provide updated guidance on educational levels to 
  8567  ensure consistency across components and with ED.
  8568      DHS appreciates commenters' concerns about the rule's effect on 
  8569  academic growth of students. DHS recognizes academic pathways can be 
  8570  complex and that students may pursue multiple degrees or transition 
  8571  programs, including from undergraduate to graduate studies. The 
  8572  Department does not intend to discourage academic advancement or 
  8573  require students to abandon years of work.
  8574      DHS also recognizes the different approaches for undergraduate

tools.name: fr_search

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".
query.title: Query

doc_type.description: Document types: RULE, PRORULE (proposed rule), NOTICE, PRESDOCU (presidential document). null for all.
doc_type.title: Doc Type

agency.description: Agency slugs, e.g. homeland-security-department, u-s-citizenship-and-immigration-services, u-s-immigration-and-customs-enforcement, state-department, labor-department, executive-office-of-the-president.
agency.title: Agency

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).
pres_type.title: Pres Type

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.
cfr.title: Cfr

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...
answer.title: Answer

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.
basis.title: Basis

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty

 16290      In the final rule, DHS added a clarifying sentence to address 
 16291  situations where F-1 students end their study or training early. For 
 16292  example, an F-1 student may enter their program anticipating it will 
 16293  take 4 years to complete, but they may then complete that program in 3 
 16294  years. Or an F-1 student may enter their program anticipating it will 
 16295  take 4 years to complete, but they may stop their studies completely 
 16296  after one semester. When an F-1 student ends their study or training 
 16297  early, that student, and any eligible dependents, must, within 30 days 
 16298  from the new end date, depart the United States or otherwise seek to 
 16299  maintain lawful status. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v).
 16300      Since an F-1 student now has 30 days, rather than the previously 
 16301  allotted 60 days, to depart the country or to otherwise maintain status 
 16302  after their completion of their program or program end date, it follows 
 16303  that they need to file a Form I-765 or successor form for post-
 16304  completion OPT within 30 days, rather than the previously allotted 60 
 16305  days, after their program end date. See new 8 CFR 
 16306  214.2(f)(11)(i)(B)(2). This has been retained in the final rule.
 16307      It similarly follows that a student may not request a start date of 
 16308  OPT employment which is more than 30 days (rather than 60 days) after 
 16309  the student's program end date. DHS overlooked this update to 8 CFR 
 16310  214.2(f)(11)(i)(D) in the NPRM but has made the change in the final 
 16311  rule. As explained in the response to comments above, DHS recognizes 
 16312  failing to make this update may cause confusion. This technical change 
 16313  aligns with the 30-day period that was proposed in the NPRM under 8 CFR 
 16314  214.2(f)(11)(i)(B)(2) and with the 30-day period of preparation for 
 16315  departure under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v).
 16316      In the NPRM, DHS also proposed retaining the current regulatory 
 16317  language that allows a 15-day period for departure from the United 
 16318  States if an alien is authorized by the DSO to withdraw from classes, 
 16319  but no additional time for departure if the alien fails to maintain a 
 16320  full course of study without the approval of the DSO or otherwise fails 
 16321  to maintain status. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v). Because DSOs 
 16322  generally authorize withdrawal based on compelling academic or medical 
 16323  circumstances when a student proactively requests permission, DHS 
 16324  believes retaining the 15-day period is appropriate and has retained 
 16325  this provision in the final rule. However, aliens who fail to maintain 
 16326  their full course of study, are denied EOS, or
 16327  
 16328  [[Page 45106]]
 16329  
 16330  otherwise violate their status are required to immediately depart the 
 16331  United States, as is consistent with other nonimmigrant 
 16332  classifications. DHS considered allowing a short ``grace period'' for 
 16333  departure after an EOS denial but concluded there was not a compelling 
 16334  reason to treat F nonimmigrants who have received a denial more 
 16335  favorably than other nonimmigrant classifications. As in other 
 16336  nonimmigrant classifications, failure to immediately depart under these 
 16337  circumstances may result in accrual of unlawful presence and subject 
 16338  the individual to removal.
 16339  4. Automatic Extension of Authorized Period of Stay and Employment
 16340  a. Authorized Period of Stay and Employment Authorization Under 8 CFR 
 16341  214.2(f)(5)(viii)
 16342      Each year, a number of U.S. employers seek to employ F-1 students 
 16343  and file a Form I-129, Petition for a Nonimmigrant Worker, with USCIS, 
 16344  along with a change of status request, to obtain classification of the 
 16345  F-1 student as an H-1B nonimmigrant worker. The H-1B nonimmigrant visa 
 16346  program allows U.S. employers to temporarily employ foreign workers in 
 16347  specialty occupations, defined by statute as occupations that require 
 16348  the theoretical and practical application of a body of highly 
 16349  specialized knowledge and a bachelor's or higher degree in the specific 
 16350  specialty, or its equivalent. See INA sections 101(a)(15)(H)(i)(b) and 
 16351  214(i); 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(15)(H)(i)(b) and 1184(i). The H-1B 
 16352  classification, however, is subject to annual numerical allocations, 
 16353  commonly referred to as a ``cap.'' See INA sections 214(g)(1)(A) and 
 16354  (g)(5)(C); 8 U.S.C. 1184(g)(1)(A) and (g)(5)(C).\323\ For purposes of 
 16355  the H-1B numerical allocations, each fiscal year begins on October 1. 
 16356  Petitioners may not file H-1B petitions more than 6 months before the 
 16357  date of actual need for the employee.\324\ Thus, the earliest date an 
 16358  H-1B cap-subject petition may be filed for an allocation for a given 
 16359  fiscal year is April 1, 6 months prior to the start of the applicable 
 16360  fiscal year for which initial H-1B classification is sought.
 16361  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16362  
 16363      \323\ Under INA 214(g)(1)(A), 8 U.S.C. 1184(g)(1)(A), 65,000 
 16364  aliens may be issued H-1B visas or otherwise provided H-1B 
 16365  nonimmigrant status in a fiscal year. This limitation does not apply 
 16366  to aliens who have earned a master's or higher degree from a U.S. 
 16367  institution of higher education, as defined in 20 U.S.C. 1001(a), 
 16368  until the number of aliens who are exempted from such numerical 
 16369  limitation during such year exceeds 20,000. INA 214(g)(5)(C), 8 
 16370  U.S.C. 1184(g)(5)(C).
 16371      \324\ See 8 CFR 214.2(h)(2)(i)(I).
 16372  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16373  
 16374      Many F-1 students complete a program of study or post-completion 
 16375  OPT in mid-spring or early summer. Per existing regulations, after 
 16376  completing their program or post-completion OPT, F-1 students have 60 
 16377  days (which DHS is proposing to change to 30 days) to take the steps 
 16378  necessary to maintain legal status or depart the United States. See new 
 16379  8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v). However, because the change to H-1B status cannot 
 16380  occur until October 1, an F-1 student whose program or post-completion 
 16381  OPT expires in mid-spring has two or more months following the 60-day 
 16382  period before the authorized period of H-1B status can commence. To 
 16383  address this situation, commonly known as the ``cap-gap,'' DHS 
 16384  established regulations that automatically extended F-1 D/S and, if 
 16385  applicable, post-completion OPT employment authorization for certain F-
 16386  1 nonimmigrants until April 1 of the fiscal year for which the H-1B 
 16387  status is being requested or until the validity start date of the 
 16388  approved petition, whichever is earlier. See redesignated 8 CFR 
 16389  214.2(f)(5)(vii). The extension of F-1 D/S and OPT employment 
 16390  authorization is commonly known as the ``cap-gap extension.'' This rule 
 16391  does not change the ``cap-gap extension'' provisions; it simply removes 
 16392  the reference to D/S and makes clear that an automatic extension will 
 16393  be granted to those with a fixed period of stay.
 16394  b. F-1 Status and Authorized Employment While EOS and/or Employment 
 16395  Authorization Applications Are Pending
 16396      DHS struck ``duration of status'' from redesignated 8 CFR 
 16397  214.2(f)(5)(vii) in the proposed rule and clarified that an alien with 
 16398  F-1 status whose admission period as indicated on his or her I-94 has 
 16399  expired, but who has timely filed an EOS application, will be 
 16400  authorized to continue pursuing a full course of study after the end 
 16401  date of his or her admission until USCIS adjudicates the EOS 
 16402  application. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii). This change allows for 
 16403  ongoing authorization to continue studies as long as the student has 
 16404  timely filed his or her EOS and will not penalize students if USCIS is 
 16405  unable to adjudicate an EOS application before a student's new term or 
 16406  course of study is underway. In such cases, students will be able to 
 16407  continue pursuing their full course of study.\325\ This change is 
 16408  retained in the final rule.
 16409  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16410  
 16411      \325\ However, if the extension of stay application is received 
 16412  during the 30-day period under new paragraph 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v), 
 16413  the F-1 student is authorized to continue a full course of study but 
 16414  may not continue or begin engaging in practical training or other 
 16415  employment. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B).
 16416  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16417  
 16418      DHS did clarify the title of new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii) in the 
 16419  final rule, since the automatic extension is for the authorized period 
 16420  of stay while the EOS is adjudicated, rather than an automatic EOS. The 
 16421  title changed from ``Automatic Extension of F stay and employment 
 16422  authorization. . .'' to ``Automatic extension of the authorized period 
 16423  of stay and employment authorization. . .''
 16424      The shift to a fixed date of admission has implications for various 
 16425  types of employment authorization. Prior to the effective date of this 
 16426  final rule, DSOs could authorize certain types of employment 
 16427  authorization, including on-campus employment and CPT,\326\ and 
 16428  students generally did not need to be concerned about a specific 
 16429  expiration date for their student status, and thus their employment 
 16430  authorization, because they were admitted for D/S. This rule changes 
 16431  that framework with different implications for various types of 
 16432  employment authorization.
 16433  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16434  
 16435      \326\ See 8 CFR 214.2(f)(9)-(12), 8 CFR 274a.12(b)(6)(iv).
 16436  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16437  
 16438      For on-campus employment where no EAD is needed, DHS is allowing 
 16439  aliens in F-1 status to continue to be authorized for on-campus 
 16440  employment while their EOS applications with USCIS are pending, not to 
 16441  exceed a period of 240 days.\327\ See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii). If 
 16442  the EOS application is still pending after 240 days have passed, the F-
 16443  1 student will no longer be authorized for employment and will need to 
 16444  stop engaging in on-campus employment. DHS is allowing a 240-day 
 16445  automatic extension period in order to minimize disruptions to on-
 16446  campus employment by teaching assistants, post-graduates working on 
 16447  research projects, and other positions that are integral to an F-1 
 16448  student's educational program. Note that the 240 days start after the 
 16449  expiration of one's current stay. DHS has always encouraged and will 
 16450  continue to encourage all nonimmigrants to apply for EOS within
 16451  
 16452  [[Page 45107]]
 16453  
 16454  the six months \328\ preceding the expiration of their current 
 16455  authorized stay thereby providing an additional buffer against any 
 16456  disruption of the ability to work.
 16457  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16458  
 16459      \327\ See 8 CFR 214.2(f)(9)(i) for a description of on-campus 
 16460  employment. For on-campus employment that is based on severe 
 16461  economic hardship resulting from emergent circumstances pursuant to 
 16462  redesignated 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(vi), see later discussion for 
 16463  additional restrictions. The EOS application must be timely filed 
 16464  pursuant to the new paragraph at 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B). 
 16465  Moreover, if an F-1 student files an extension of stay application 
 16466  during the 30-day period provided in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v)(new), he 
 16467  or she does not receive an automatic extension of authorized 
 16468  employment, including on-campus, CPT, and severe economic hardship,

 16472      \328\ With respect to the earliest filing date for a Form I-539, 
 16473  there is no prohibition on filing the form before a certain date 
 16474  ahead of expiration.
 16475  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16476  
 16477      Likewise, DHS is allowing an automatic extension of off-campus 
 16478  employment authorization for up to 240-days during the pendency of the 
 16479  EOS application, for F-1 students who have demonstrated severe economic 
 16480  hardship pursuant to 8 CFR 214.2(f)(9)(ii)(C) and previously received 
 16481  an EAD from USCIS that expired at the program end date that is now 
 16482  being extended with the EOS application. See new 8 CFR 
 16483  214.2(f)(5)(viii). These circumstances may include loss of financial 
 16484  aid or on-campus employment without fault on the part of the student, 
 16485  substantial fluctuations in the value of currency or exchange rate, 
 16486  inordinate increases in tuition and/or living costs, unexpected changes 
 16487  in the financial condition of the student's source of support, medical 
 16488  bills, or other substantial and unexpected expenses. In such cases, DHS 
 16489  believes a 240-day automatic extension of employment authorization will 
 16490  help alleviate the severe economic hardship and avoid a disruption in

 16498  
 16499      \329\ See 8 CFR 274a.12(c)(3). 8 CFR 214.2(f)(9)(ii)(F)(2) 
 16500  provides that employment authorization based upon severe economic 
 16501  hardship may be granted in one-year intervals up to the expected

 16506  basis of severe economic hardship resulting from emergent circumstances
